In adults, the condition is called osteomalacia. • Calcium and phosphate are both low because vitamin D is needed for intestinal absorption of both. • PTH goes up because calcium is low (decreased negative feedback). • It should be noted that in vitamin D deficiency caused by renal failure, phosphate is high, not low, because the effect of the renal failure on phosphate levels wins over the mere vitamin D deficiency. In renal failure, the kidney cannot downregulate the PCT phosphate reabsorption channels, thereby increasing absorption. • Never choose low phosphate in renal failure, even though vitamin D3 activation is low. • Renal failure + low vitamin D: o ↓ serum Ca2+ , ↑ serum PO43- , ↑ PTH. • No renal failure + low vitamin D (i.e., rickets/osteomalacia): o ↓ serum Ca2+ , ↓ serum PO43- , ↑ PTH.
rapidFireQAs.explanation: Diagnosis is rickets (vitamin D deficiency in children). In adults, the condition is called osteomalacia. • Calcium and phosphate are both low because vitamin D is needed for intestinal absorption of both. • PTH goes up because calcium is low (decreased negative feedback). • It should be noted that in vitamin D deficiency caused by renal failure, phosphate is high, not low, because the effect of the renal failure on phosphate levels wins over the mere vitamin D deficiency. In renal failure, the kidney cannot downregulate the PCT phosphate reabsorption channels, thereby increasing absorption. • Never choose low phosphate in renal failure, even though vitamin D3 activation is low. • Renal failure + low vitamin D: o ↓ serum Ca2+ , ↑ serum PO43- , ↑ PTH. • No renal failure + low vitamin D (i.e., rickets/osteomalacia): o ↓ serum Ca2+ , ↓ serum PO43- , ↑ PTH.

rapidFireQAs.q: 77F + bone densitometry shows bone density of hips and vertebrae >2.5 standard deviations below the mean for 20-yr-old women. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for serum Ca2+ , serum PO43-, PTH, and 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ Serum Ca2+ , ↔ serum PO43- , ↔ PTH, ↔ 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3. — Diagnosis is osteoporosis. All laboratory findings will be normal. • Students often get this question wrong, assuming, e.g., calcium must be low, but serum findings are completely normal for most patients. • USMLE question will often be in graph form, with calcium on the x-axis and PTH on the y-axis, with letters at different locations. The correct answer here is simply the letter in the normal range for both calcium and PTH.
rapidFireQAs.explanation: Diagnosis is osteoporosis. All laboratory findings will be normal. • Students often get this question wrong, assuming, e.g., calcium must be low, but serum findings are completely normal for most patients. • USMLE question will often be in graph form, with calcium on the x-axis and PTH on the y-axis, with letters at different locations. The correct answer here is simply the letter in the normal range for both calcium and PTH.

rapidFireQAs.q: 15F + asymptomatic + cardiac auscultation reveals fixed splitting of the S2 heart sound. Compared to normal values, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for superior vena cava pO2, right atrial pO2, right ventricular pO2, and pulmonary artery pO2?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ Superior vena cava pO2, ↑ right atrial pO2, ↑ right ventricular pO2, ↑ pulmonary artery pO2. — Diagnosis is atrial septal defect (ASD). • Since the defect is between the atria, and pressures are greater on the left side of the heart than the right, oxygenated blood from the LA will move into the RA, thereby increasing the RA chamber pO2 compared to normal. This higher pO2 will carry through to the RV and then to the pulmonary arteries. • Vena cava pO2 is unchanged because the SVC and IVC are prior to the defect. • The USMLE usually gives this type of Q in the reverse direction – i.e., they’ll list a bunch of chamber oxygen values and expect you to be able to infer the type of defect (i.e., ASD or VSD).
rapidFireQAs.explanation: Diagnosis is atrial septal defect (ASD). • Since the defect is between the atria, and pressures are greater on the left side of the heart than the right, oxygenated blood from the LA will move into the RA, thereby increasing the RA chamber pO2 compared to normal. This higher pO2 will carry through to the RV and then to the pulmonary arteries. • Vena cava pO2 is unchanged because the SVC and IVC are prior to the defect. • The USMLE usually gives this type of Q in the reverse direction – i.e., they’ll list a bunch of chamber oxygen values and expect you to be able to infer the type of defect (i.e., ASD or VSD).

rapidFireQAs.q: Student Q showed electron micrograph (EM) pic of sarcomere + they asked what does not change length during muscle contraction + had letters at different locations. Answer = A-band.
rapidFireQAs.a: Before you instantly freak out, relax. First look at above EM of sarcomere. Then compare with bottom images here: All you need to know is: as the myosin and actin overlap during muscle contraction, the H- zone, I-band, and sarcomere (Z-Z) shorten. The A-band (myosin; neon-green bar above) does not change in length. Tropomyosin is a protein on actin that covers up myosin binding sites. During contraction, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and binds to troponin, causing a conformational change that releases tropomyosin from actin, thereby allowing myosin to bind. ATP is required to relax muscle (i.e., rigor mortis in the deceased due to ↓ ATP).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + partakes in research study of muscle contraction; Q asks, on the following electron micrograph of a sarcomere, which segment will not change length? (choose the number):
rapidFireQAs.a: #2 (A-band). In contrast, the I-band (#6), H-zone (#7), and length of sarcomere (#1; Z-Z) all shorten during contraction.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31M + in wilderness for 3 weeks without food; Q asks what allows him to maintain normal serum glucose levels during this time; answer = “skeletal muscle protein”
rapidFireQAs.a: you must know that skeletal muscle does not contain glucose-6-phosphatase and therefore does not directly carry out gluconeogenesis; glucogenic amino acids can be liberated in the fasting state from skeletal muscle, with the liver carrying out the gluconeogenesis. The kidney can also carry out gluconeogenesis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Q on offline Step 1 NBME form asks why ATP does not fall appreciably during a series of muscle twitches
rapidFireQAs.a: “ATP is quickly regenerating from creatine phosphate.”

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about shoulder anatomy for USMLE?”
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE is known to occasionally give images of shoulder, clavicular, and humeral fractures. Spending a few moments to gain an idea of normal shoulder anatomy is not “nitpicky.”

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about the rotator cuff? It’s high-yield right?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Yes. Same as with the above x-rays, you need to know the rotator cuff muscles. Just deal with it.

rapidFireQAs.q: Empty-can (thumb-down) / full-can (thumb-up) tests for diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: patient abducts arm to 90 degrees with thumbs up or down → downward pressure applied to arm → if elicits pain, answer = supraspinatus injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: Gerber lift-off test = patient places dorsal aspect of hand on lower back, with palm facing posteriorly
rapidFireQAs.a: examiner applies pressure into the patient’s palm against his/her lower back → patient is then asked to move hand away under the pressure → if elicits pain / difficult to do, answer = subscapularis injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Are there other shoulder conditions sometimes confused with rotator cuff injury?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Yes. USMLE likes subacromial bursitis and biceps tendonitis as well. Frequently confused shoulder conditions for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: “I know upper limb nerves are HY. What do I need to know for USMLE without all of the .”
rapidFireQAs.a: You need to know the injuries associated with the nerves, and then just basic motor/sensory issues. Upper limb nerve HY Points for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + construction worker + sensation to pinprick is reduced on the thumb and a portion of the forearm; physician suspects compression of C5/C6; Q asks, which movement is most likely impaired in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: “abduction of upper extremity”; deltoid is innervated by axillary nerve from C5/C6.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + office worker + paresthesias of lateral three fingers; wrist pad when using computer and wrist splint have not worked; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: triamcinolone injection into carpal tunnel; NSAIDs are wrong answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49F + skiing accident + decreased sensation over lateral forearm + weakened flexion at elbow; Q asks nerve that’s impaired
rapidFireQAs.a: musculocutaneous.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35M + in car accident and wasn’t wearing seatbelt + x-ray of arm is shown below; Q wants to know the most likely deficit in this patient:
rapidFireQAs.a: inability to extend the wrist; answer can also be inability to supinate the forearm; x-ray shows midshaft fracture of humerus → radial nerve injury resulting in pronated arm with wrist drop.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29F + motorcycle accident + has x-ray of arm shown below; Q asks most likely deficit to be seen in this patient:
rapidFireQAs.a: impaired abduction of arm, or loss of sensation over deltoid; x-ray shows surgical neck of humerus fracture → axillary nerve injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + has arm slashed in street fight + now is unable to supinate and extend wrist; which letter on the following brachial plexus image corresponds to this patient’s deficit?
rapidFireQAs.a: radial nerve (choice C). A = musculocutaneous nerve; B = axillary nerve; D = median nerve; E = ulnar nerve. USMLE will ask you relatively easy presentation for a neurologic deficit but require you to identify where on the brachial plexus is affected.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + in motorcycle accident + has loss of sensation over deltoid + diminished ability to abduct shoulder; question asked which nerve on the following diagram is impaired.
rapidFireQAs.a: E (axillary nerve); A = musculocutaneous nerve; B = median nerve; C = ulnar nerve; D = radial nerve; F = long thoracic nerve; the black lines on the left side of the above image, from top to bottom, are the C5-T1 nerve roots.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Does USMLE care about upper limb reflexes?”
rapidFireQAs.a: They do show up on NBME, yes. You could be aware that if biceps reflex is weakened, they want C5 as the nerve root that’s impaired. And if triceps reflex is weakened, it’s C6-7 that’s impaired.

rapidFireQAs.q: 14-month-old boy + arm has been adducted, pronated, and wrist flexed since birth but has gradually been improving with physiotherapy; Q asks location of injury
rapidFireQAs.a: upper brachial plexus (C5- C6); Erb-Duchenne palsy presents with “waiter’s tip” deformity; most commonly seen in neonates during traumatic birth, but can also occur in older patients due to trauma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + grabbed onto tree branch while falling from tree + presents with claw-like appearance of hand; Q wants to know location of injury
rapidFireQAs.a: lower brachial plexus (C8-T1); you just need to know Klumpke palsy = lower brachial plexus injury and presents with claw-hand.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49F + underwent mastectomy one year ago + physical examination demonstrates winged scapula; Q asks nerve injury; answer = long thoracic nerve
rapidFireQAs.a: innervates serratus anterior; nerve can be damaged during mastectomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + paresthesias of the hand and forearm + sometimes exacerbated by wearing backpack for long periods; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: thoracic outlet syndrome; common cause is “first cervical rib.” USMLE just wants you to know there’s some strange anatomic variant of the cervical ribs where a “first cervical rib” can cause miscellaneous paresthesias and/or muscle wasting of upper limb. This is called thoracic outlet syndrome. Nothing else you need to know.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F + was painting fence + pain in anterior/lateral shoulder that is worse when lying on side in bed + no weakness in shoulder; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: subacromial bursitis (impingement syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F + was painting fence + pain in anterior/lateral shoulder that is worse when lying on side in bed + weakness on external rotation of shoulder; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: rotator cuff tendonitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26M + pain in anterior shoulder + palpation of anterior shoulder elicits pain; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: biceps tendonitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about bones of hand / wrist?” → USMLE likes carpal bones.
rapidFireQAs.a: The two rows of carpal bones (i.e., proximal and distal), from lateral to medial, are: “She Looks Too Pretty. Try To Catch Her.” § First row: Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform; § Second row: Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + skateboarding + falls on outstretched hand + no pain over anatomic snuffbox + pain in central palm; Q asks which bone is fractured (choose a letter):
rapidFireQAs.a: D (lunate); this is on Step 1 NBME; as described, they’ll give pain in central palm + no pain over anatomic snuffbox.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + skateboarding + falls on outstretched hand + pain over anatomic snuffbox + x-ray shows no abnormalities; Q asks which bone is fractured:
rapidFireQAs.a: C (scaphoid); next best step is thumb-spica cast; x-ray is often negative initially; patient needs thumb-spica cast to prevent avascular necrosis, followed by re-x-ray in 2-3 weeks.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17F + injured index finger at softball game + can’t flex distal interphalangeal joint of right index finger; Q wants to know which tendon is most likely damaged → answer = flexor digitorum profundus; USMLE wants you to know that flexor digitorum superficialis does not flex the DIPs, but flexor digitorum profundus does.
rapidFireQAs.a: “Wait, are you saying we need to know all about hand/forearm muscles and tendons, etc. then?” → No. USMLE really doesn’t tests hyper-nitpicky details, but I’ve seen this one asked on an offline Step 1 NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + hunting accident in which he sustains gunshot wound and severs flexor digitorum profundus tendon; Q asks which forearm tendon can be used as a graft to repair the damaged tendon
rapidFireQAs.a: palmaris longus; classically used as graft tendon; not present in about 1/7 people in the population.

rapidFireQAs.q: 59M + alcoholic + smoker + worked in construction + image of hand shown below; Q wants to know biggest risk factor in this patient:
rapidFireQAs.a: alcoholism; diagnosis is Dupuytren contracture, which is abnormal proliferation of palmar connective tissue and fascia; risk factors are Norwegian descent, alcoholism, diabetes, and epilepsy. Constellation of risk factors makes no sense, but just memorize it.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + breastfeeding + severe pain in lateral wrist; pain is worsened with maneuver shown below; Q asks for the next step in management
rapidFireQAs.a: steroid injection; diagnosis is deQuervain tenosynovitis; tenosynovitis means inflammation of tendon sheaths; deQuervain is classic in breastfeeding women and is worsened with Finkelstein test (shown above) → 1) thumb is placed in palm; 2) 2nd -5th fingers are wrapped over the palm; 3) patient ulnar deviates the wrist → this causes pain. Patient should avoid offending activity, but since this is often breastfeeding, steroid injection can provide immediate relief.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + painless 2-cm bump on dorsal aspect of hand/wrist + image shown below; Q wants diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: ganglion cyst, which is gelatinous collection of joint fluid; Tx is observation. Needle drainage is only done if causing functional/cosmetic issues for the patient. Recurrence common; can occur on ankles and flexor areas as well, but classic location is dorsum of hand/wrist. Offline NBME Q asks for most likely outcome of this pathology if untreated, and answer = “spontaneous regression.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + history of easy bruising + hyperextensible skin + image shown below; Q wants to know mechanism:
rapidFireQAs.a: “defect in synthesis of fibrillar collagen”; diagnosis is Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (usually caused by collagen III defect); wrong answer = “abnormal synthesis of extracellular glycoprotein” (refers to fibrillin, which is a glycoprotein that forms a sheath around/stabilizes elastin); do not confuse fibrillar collagen (Ehlers-Danlos) with fibrillin (Marfan syndrome). Marfan syndrome has nothing to do with collagen.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54F + smoker past 40 years + bilateral hand pain with clubbing; Q wants next best step in diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: chest x-ray; Dx is hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (osteoarthropathia hypertrophicans); presents as arthritis + clubbing as a result of lung cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Do I need to know hip dislocation stuff? I’ve seen an occasional question like that but don’t really get it?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Not super-high-yield, but you just need to know that posterior hip dislocation causes a shortened and internally rotated leg; anterior hip dislocation causes a shortened and externally rotated leg.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What are some HY things I need to know about MSK spinal stuff?”
rapidFireQAs.a: I talk about neuro-related stuff a lot more in my HY Neuroanatomy PDF, but below is a table of some HY MSK spinal stuff. HY MSK spinal conditions for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know for cauda equina syndrome versus conus medullaris syndrome?”
rapidFireQAs.a: The spinal cord ends at L1-L2. The terminal cone of the spinal cord is the conus medullaris. The nerve fibers that branch from the spinal cord and run inferior to it are the cauda equina. Resources make these conditions way more complicated than they need to be. For USMLE, all they really care about is: both conditions can cause urinary retention and pain in the legs; conus medullaris syndrome is sudden-onset (think cone is “sharp”) and causes perianal anesthesia; cauda equina syndrome is gradual-onset and causes saddle anesthesia. If you look these conditions up online, you’ll see numerous differences listed side by side. Waste of time for USMLE. USMLE likes breast, prostate, and lung metastases to the spine as important cause of cauda equina syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + painful neck + no neurologic findings + elective MRI shows degenerative changes of cervical spine; Q asks most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical spondylosis; this is merely osteoarthritic degenerative changes to the cervical vertebrae; it is idiopathic, but often has familial association.

rapidFireQAs.q: 63M + pain in buttocks and thighs when walking + no cardiovascular disease + peripheral pulses normal; Q wants to know diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: lumbar spinal stenosis; this presentation is “neurogenic claudication,” where the vignette sounds like intermittent claudication due to aortoiliac atherosclerosis, but the patient will have no cardiovascular disease history and they’ll say peripheral pulses are normal; this is due to osteoarthritic changes in the lumbar spine.

rapidFireQAs.q: 67M + lower back pain worse when standing or walking for 30 minutes + relieved when leaning forward; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: lumbar spinal stenosis; classically pain in lower back that is worse when standing or walking for extended periods of time; it is worse when leaning back + better when leaning forward.

rapidFireQAs.q: 79F + difficulty fastening buttons + weakness of hand muscles + numbness in 5th finger; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: “C7-T1 foraminal stenosis” (cervical spinal stenosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 61F + vignette is big rambling paragraph of nonsense + they tell you there’s a “step-off” of one vertebra relative to another on palpation; Q wants to know diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: spondylolisthesis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 48F + gardening + sudden-onset severe pain down right leg + straight-leg test elicits radiating pain; Q asks what is most likely to confirm diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: MRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: 48F + gardening + sudden-onset severe pain down right leg + straight-leg test elicits radiating pain; Q asks most appropriate treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: “analgesics + exercise as tolerated”; analgesics = NSAIDs; bed-rest is wrong answer on USMLE for both lumbosacral strain and disc herniations.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + high BMI + 24-hour history of pain starting in lower back and shooting down left leg; Q wants treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAIDs; Dx is sciatica; 90% of the time due to disc herniation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55F + pain + paresthesias in lateral thigh + no history of trauma; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: meralgia paresthetica.

rapidFireQAs.q: 74M + lifted heavy suitcases around the house + sudden-onset pain and tingling in lower back + suprapubic mass + has not urinated for past 24 hours + perianal anesthesia; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: conus medullaris syndrome; findings tend to be sudden-onset (cone is “sharp”/sudden); perianal anesthesia is characteristic; both conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes can present with urinary retention and pain in the lower back / legs.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Do I need to know dermatomes for USMLE?”
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE doesn’t crazy-obsess, but you need to have an idea of the basics → C6 is thumb; C7 is middle finger; C8 is pinky; nipples are T4; umbilicus is T10; groin and lower back are L1; anteromedial leg is L4; sole of foot is S1.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57F + burning/itching pain along lower back close to the hip on the left; Q asks which dermatome this represents (answers are T10, L1, S1)
rapidFireQAs.a: L1; diagnosis is shingles (herpes zoster; VZV).

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about lower limb reflexes / radiculopathies?
rapidFireQAs.a: ” Lower limb reflexes / radiculopathies

rapidFireQAs.q: 41F + pain radiating down distal anterior thigh, knee, medial leg, and medial foot; compression of nerve root in which intervertebral foramina is most likely the cause of her symptoms?
41F + random leg sensory issues + knee jerk is impaired; Q asks nerve root
41F + random leg sensory issues + ankle jerk is impaired; Q asks nerve root
41F + big paragraph of nonsense + loss of sensation of sole of foot; Q asks nerve root
65F + gradual-onset inability to stand on the tippytoes + diminished sensation on sole of the foot + MRI is shown below; Q wants most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Disc herniation of L5-S1; USMLE doesn’t expect you to be a radiology expert; the diagnosis is inferable based on the vignette alone; MRI shows herniation of nucleus pulposus of L5-S1 disc with impingement on the spinal cord.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Do I need to know ankle sprain stuff for USMLE?” → For both USMLE Step 1 Family Medicine, yes.
rapidFireQAs.a: Anterior talofibular ligament is on the lateral side of the ankle and will be injured if the foot inverts (rolls inward). This is the most commonly injured ankle ligament. The deltoid ligament is stronger and on the medial side of the ankle. This injury is more rare and occurs if the ankle forcibly everts (rolls outward). There is a Q on one of the Step 1 NBME exams where they show some arcane x-ray of the ankle + tell you the patient had forcible eversion of the ankle + they ask what’s injured → answer = deltoid ligament.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + playing basketball + lands on right ankle where it forcibly everts; x-ray is shown below; left side of x-ray shows prior to ligamental repair; right side is after repair; Q asks which ligament is injured:
rapidFireQAs.a: deltoid ligament; notice the large joint space on the medial aspect of the ankle in the left x-ray.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + went running and rolled her ankle + pain in lateral ankle + tenderness posterior to malleolus + can bear weight; Q wants next best step
rapidFireQAs.a: x-ray of ankle; patient fulfills Ottawa criteria for x-ray → she has pain in malleolar region + tenderness posterior to the malleolus; although she can bear weight, the former two findings satisfy the Ottawa criteria.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Does USMLE care about knowing all of the muscles and their insertions/origins, etc.?” → USMLE does have random Qs where they show MRI cross-sections of the thigh:
rapidFireQAs.a: 1 = rectus femoris; 2 = vastus lateralis; 3 = vastus intermedius; 4 = vastus medialis; 5 = sartorius; 6 = biceps femoris short head; 7 = biceps femoris long head; 8 = semimembranosus; 9 = semitendinosis; 10 = adductor magnus; 11 = adductor longus; 12 = adductor brevis; 13 = gracilis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + plays soccer + pain in the leg + MRI cross-section shows muscle that’s injured; Q asks which muscle it is:
rapidFireQAs.a: rectus femoris.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about the arthritis conditions for USMLE?
rapidFireQAs.a: ” HY Arthritides / joint pathologies for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: 49F + left knee pain + BMI 40 + Q asks what would most likely have prevented this patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: weight loss; diagnosis is osteoarthritis (OA). As easy as it gets, but this Q is rampant on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + 6’2” + right knee pain + BMI 30; Q asks, in addition to weight loss, what is the most appropriate treatment for this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: acetaminophen; diagnosis is OA; patient here is young, but big and tall; NSAID as first answer is wrong. As I mentioned above, OA is non-inflammatory, so NSAIDs don’t help more than acetaminophen + they kill the kidney.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29F + history of intermittent wrist and knee pain + presents today with fever 101 F and a hot, red, painful knee; Q wants next best step in diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: arthrocentesis; diagnosis is septic arthritis in patient with underlying RA.

rapidFireQAs.q: 59M + pain in his hands + x-ray is shown below; Q asks the mechanism for this patient’s condition:
rapidFireQAs.a: “degenerative joint disease”; diagnosis is OA; image is showing Heberden nodes. If you look at x-ray, the DIPs “look a little swollen”; if you get a hand x-ray like this on USMLE and have no idea what you’re looking at, just ask yourself, “Do the DIPs looked impaired in any way?” → if yes, answer is definitely not RA, and is probably OA.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + walks in bent over at the waist with chest pain + painful wrists and knee + hemoglobin of 10 g/dL; Q asks how to treat the patient’s hematologic findings
rapidFireQAs.a: “no specific therapy indicated”; patient has RA; autoimmune diseases can present with serous pericarditis (patient bends / leans forward to relieve chest pain) and anemia of chronic disease; even though we treat the underlying condition (i.e., the RA in this case), I’ve seen NBME write “no specific therapy indicated” for anemia of chronic disease in this situation; do not give EPO for AoCD unless the etiology is renal failure. EPO is wrong answer otherwise.

rapidFireQAs.q: 51M + advanced rheumatoid arthritis + paresthesias of upper limbs; Q asks next step in diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: MRI of cervical spine; Q has nothing to do with surgery, but upper limb neurologic findings in RA patient suggest atlantoaxial subluxation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + sore wrists and knee + diffuse pruritis + high serum cholesterol, direct bilirubin, and ALP; Q asks for treatment of jaundice
rapidFireQAs.a: ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol); patient has rheumatoid arthritis and primary biliary cirrhosis; remember that “autoimmune diseases go together”; USMLE also wants you to know MOA of ursodiol is “decreased secretion of cholesterol into bile).

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + low back pain worse in the morning and gets better throughout the day + occasional hand pain; Q wants to know next step in diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: x-ray of sacroiliac joints; diagnosis is ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis; both are linked via HLA-B27 (PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 29M + back pain worse in morning and gets better throughout the day + x-ray of spine shown below; Q wants to know next step in management?
rapidFireQAs.a: slit-lamp examination; diagnosis is ankylosing spondylitis with x-ray showing bamboo spine; USMLE wants you to know annual slit-lamp examination for anterior uveitis is part of workup.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28M + silvery, scaly plaque on elbow + scraping of the plaque causes bleeding; Q asks for the most appropriate treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: topical calcipotriene (vitamin D derivative); Tx of psoriasis is topicals first → topical calcipotriene, or topical steroids (triamcinolone or hydrocortisone), or coal tar, usually in that order.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + long history of plaque psoriasis that responds well to topicals + has increasing hand pain over past year + x-ray shown below; Q wants to know the most appropriate treatment:
rapidFireQAs.a: methotrexate; x-ray shows pencil-in-cup deformity of DIP of 2nd digit; methotrexate is first-line oral agent for systemic psoriasis (psoriatic arthritis), or if patient has unremitting plaque psoriasis that fails topicals.

rapidFireQAs.q: 39M + long history of psoriasis that does not respond to topicals; Q asks for oral treatment + methotrexate is not listed
rapidFireQAs.a: acitretin (oral vitamin A derivative used for psoriasis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 9F + painful knee + has had a few episodes similar to this before + hemoglobin 10 g/dL + MCV 72; Q asks most likely hematologic diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: anemia of chronic disease due to JRA; you need to know that MCV can absolutely be low in AoCD; this is

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + runny nose for 3 days + now has left hip pain + temperature is 100.5 F + hip is not erythematous or warm; patient can bear weight on the hip; Q asks for next step in management
rapidFireQAs.a: ibuprofen; diagnosis is toxic (transient) synovitis; this is viral infection that, for whatever magical reason, can cause inflammation of the hip that can be misdiagnosed as septic arthritis; recognize that this is a common condition and if septic arthritis is less likely (i.e., kid can bear weight; there is no leukocytosis; hip is not red and hot), do not draconianly stab the kid in the hip for a joint aspirate.

rapidFireQAs.q: 10M + painful left hip for 2 days + fever of 101 F + leukocytes elevated + cannot bear weight on the hip + question says nothing about warmth or redness of hip; Q asks next best step
rapidFireQAs.a: arthrocentesis; septic arthritis must be ruled out here; for these types of Qs, you have to use your intuition; remember that for toxic synovitis, they’ll usually say viral infection precedes the hip pain + no leukocytosis + patient can bear weight.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8F + intermittent knee pain and salmon-pink body rash + presents today with hot, red, painful knee with limited mobility; Q wants to know most likely diagnosis (JRA not listed)
rapidFireQAs.a: septic arthritis; as discussed earlier, JRA is a risk factor for septic arthritis, so although patient has JRA above, the acute diagnosis is SA; USMLE will often give this type of Q where they have “toxic synovitis” as a wrong answer choice (easy, since we discussed above toxic synovitis is hip pain after viral infection; toxic synovitis is never the knee); salmon-pink body rash is buzzy for JRA, but I’d say it only presents in half of NBME vignettes tops.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + arthritis of hands + low platelets + no other information; Q asks most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: SLE; you need to know lupus can present with low platelets due to antibodies causing peripheral destruction; arthritis is most common presenting feature of lupus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F + arthritis of hands + low platelets + low WBCs + low hemoglobin; Q asks mechanism for this patient’s hematologic findings
rapidFireQAs.a: “increased peripheral destruction”; wrong answer = “defective bone marrow production”; in SLE, patients can have antibodies against their hematologic cell lines; isolated thrombocytopenia is most common, but antibodies resulting in leukopenia and erythropenia also can occur; this looks like aplastic anemia (e.g., from Parvo), but it’s not.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + sore hands and knee + malar rash + question asks what’s most likely to be deficient in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: C1q; for whatever reason, complement protein C1q deficiency is a cause of lupus. Also remember that in acute flares, C3 decreases and dsDNA Abs increase.

rapidFireQAs.q: 36F + arthritis + thrombocytopenia + positive syphilis test; Q asks what’s most likely to be seen in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: antibodies against phospholipid; patients with SLE who have anti-phospholipid syndrome can have false-positive VDRL syphilis screening.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + sore knee + drinks alcohol + takes daily aspirin for ischemic heart disease; Q wants to know treatment for this patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: indomethacin; steroids are wrong answer; diagnosis is acute gout; student says, “But why do we give NSAID as Tx if patient is taking daily aspirin, which is an NSAID?” → it’s what the NBME exam wants; daily low-dose aspirin is actually a risk factor for acute gout.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + sore knee + joint aspirate shows needle-shaped crystals + patient has history of NSAID allergy; Q asks most appropriate treatment (steroids not listed)
rapidFireQAs.a: colchicine; used for acute gout in patients who can’t take NSAIDs (e.g., peptic ulcers or allergy).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + presents with swollen and painful big toe; Q asks which of the following will decrease recurrence of this patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: allopurinol; xanthine oxidase inhibitors (i.e., allopurinol or febuxostat) are first-line for chronic gout to decrease recurrence.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + being treated in hospital with IV nafcillin for MSSA endocarditis + is administered probenecid; Q asks reason for this management
rapidFireQAs.a: decreases renal clearance of beta-lactam; probenecid inhibits organic anion transporter (OAT), which both prevents reabsorption of uric acid and secretion of beta-lactams; uricosurics not used first-line for chronic gout because they increase risk of uric acid stones.

rapidFireQAs.q: 39M + left knee pain + hyperpigmentation of forearms + increased serum glucose; Q asks what is most likely to be seen on joint aspirate
rapidFireQAs.a: calcium pyrophosphate; diagnosis is pseudogout; biggest risk factors are hereditary hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism; patient here has “bronze diabetes,” which is buzzy presentation for hemochromatosis; hyperpigmentation is hemosiderin deposition; high glucose is from iron deposition in tail of pancreas.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + painful hands with soreness of DIPs + overweight + serum calcium 11 mg/dL (NR 8.4-10.2); Q asks most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudogout, not OA; pseudogout can present as an OA-like presentation in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism or hereditary hemochromatosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + painful knee + joint aspirate shows rhomboid positively birefringent crystals; Q asks most appropriate treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: indomethacin; treat acute pseudogout exactly the same as “regular” gout. However, for chronic pseudogout, treat the underlying condition.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + sore shoulder + ESR not elevated; Q asks what’s most likely to be seen on joint aspiration
rapidFireQAs.a: basic calcium phosphate → BCP crystals cause “Milwaukee shoulder,” which is a cold (non- inflammatory) shoulder effusion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28M + painful red knee + fever 102 F + went hiking for 12 hours two days ago; Q asks for the most likely organism
rapidFireQAs.a: Staph aureus; USMLE wants you to know that otherwise young, healthy patients who’ve had recent microtrauma (e.g., hiking, soccer/kickboxing tournament) or overt trauma (i.e., car accident where knee hit the dashboard) can get septic arthritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + med student + knocked up however many chicks the past year + presents with sore knee + joint aspiration shows no organisms; Q asks the most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: Gonococcal arthritis; if Q is overt about sexual activity in younger patient, they want Gonococcus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + history of rheumatoid arthritis + presents with hot, red, painful knee and fever of 102 F; Q asks most likely organism
rapidFireQAs.a: Staph aureus; if Q doesn’t emphasize unprotected sexual activity + patient has clear risk factor for SA, then S. aureus is more likely than Gonococcus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 14F + sickle cell + painful, red, hot knee; Q asks most likely organism
rapidFireQAs.a: Staph aureus; Salmonella, although a common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell, there is not increased risk of it causing septic arthritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27M + painful knee and wrist + cutaneous papules along the wrist; Q asks for the most appropriate treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: ceftriaxone + azithromycin; diagnosis is Gonococcal arthritis; HY to know it can present with cutaneous papules; must co-treat for chlamydia with azithromycin or doxycycline.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + sore hands and knees + urethral discharge + red eyes; Q asks most likely organism
rapidFireQAs.a: Chlamydia; wrong answer is Gonorrhea; reactive arthritis is classically Chlamydia; Gonococcus does not cause reactive arthritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + pain, redness, and swelling of shaft of left forearm + fever of 103 F + WBCs 14,000/µL; Q wants most likely organism
rapidFireQAs.a: Staph aureus; Dx is osteomyelitis; S. aureus is most common organism overall, especially when etiology is idiopathic.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + sickle cell disease + pain in foot for 3 weeks + fever 102 F + WBCs 14,000/µL; Q wants most likely organism
rapidFireQAs.a: Salmonella spp.; if Q gives you sickle cell with osteomyelitis, the organism they want is Salmonella. You still need to use your head though. If they say “gram-positive coccus” in patient with sickle cell, that would be Staph aureus, not Salmonella. The latter is a gram-negative rod.

rapidFireQAs.q: 47M + immigrant to USA from Albania + history of tuberculosis + pain over T9/T10 vertebrae; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: vertebral osteomyelitis (Pott disease).

rapidFireQAs.q: 28M + migrant worker + rigid abdomen + fever + holds right lower extremity in extension + PPD shows 16 mm induration; Q asks which muscle is most likely to be affected in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: psoas major; you don’t have to worry about the anatomy here; just know that TB can cause psoas abscess.

rapidFireQAs.q: 56M + IV drug user + diabetes mellitus type II + left-sided back pain radiating to flank + fever 102 F + pyelonephritis not listed as answer; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: psoas abscess; just be aware of it as a DDx; most likely organism is Staph aureus; Tx = surgical drainage + IV antibiotics. Other random joint/MSK disorders

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + left knee pain that is worse when sitting for long periods of time, or when going up or down stairs; Q asks for treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: “quadriceps strengthening exercises”; diagnosis is chrondromalacia patellae (aka patellofemoral pain syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + started playing recreational basketball two years ago + knee pain initially worse with activity but now is present even when not playing; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: patella tendonitis (“Jumper’s knee”).

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + plays volleyball + pain in knee past 6 weeks worse when running or jumping + exam shows crepitus; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: “patellofemoral instability” (patellar tendonitis / “jumper’s knee” not listed as answer); shows up on NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + Q gives big paragraph of unnecessary info + they tell you guy has lateral hip pain that is worse when palpated and while lying on his side in bed; Q just asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: trochanteric bursitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + started playing recreational basketball two years ago + knee pain worse with activity but now is present even when not playing; patient had fracture to proximal tibia 30 years ago that was treated with open reduction and internal fixation; x-ray shows varus deformity of knee; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: post-traumatic arthritis, not patella tendonitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28M + playing football + injures knee + increased anterior displacement of tibia on examination; Q wants to know what is injured on the following MRI:
rapidFireQAs.a: anterior cruciate ligament (choice B). A = femur; C = PCL; D = tibia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + painful, red, warm knee + joint aspiration shows no effusion; Q asks most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: septic bursitis; vignette will sound like septic arthritis, but there will be no effusion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 15M + plays a lot of soccer + 5’11” + painful knee; Q wants mechanism of pathology
rapidFireQAs.a: inflammation of patellar ligament at tibial tuberosity; diagnosis is Osgood-Schlatter.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + plays basketball + right heel pain for 5-10 minutes after getting out of bed in the morning; Q asks mechanism of pathology
rapidFireQAs.a: inflammation of planta fascia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + in car accident + hits her left knee on the dashboard + physical exam shows excessive posterior displacement of the tibia; Q asks for diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: PCL injury (dashboard injury).

rapidFireQAs.q: 19M + hurt his knee wakeboarding + physical exam shows excessive motion of lateral aspect of knee when pressure applied to medial knee; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: lateral collateral ligament injury; test described is the varus test.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + hurt his knee wakeboarding + medial knee pain + vignette mentions “catching” or “locking” of the knee; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: medial meniscal tear.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + BMI 30 + pain on the inner side of the left knee a few centimeters below the kneecap; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: pes anserine bursitis; the answer on USMLE if they give inferomedial knee pain.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born at term + perfectly healthy + feet bent inward; Q wants to know treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: serial casting; observation is wrong answer; diagnosis is talipes equinovarus (clubbed feet).

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born at term + clubbed feet + multiple joint contractures; Q asks for diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: arthrogryposis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + wears high-heels + has severe pain under foot along the 2nd and 3rd metatarsals; Q asks for treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: orthotics first, then steroid injection second; Dx is Morton neuroma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4-month-old boy + clicking and clunking on physical examination; Q wants next best step in imaging
rapidFireQAs.a: ultrasound; diagnosis is primary hip dysplasia; do ultrasound under 6 months; x-ray over 6 months.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4-month-old girl + clicking and clunking on physical exam; Q asks for mechanism of patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: “poorly developed acetabulum.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 5M + right hip pain + walks with limp + x-ray shows contracted capital femoral epiphysis; Q asks straight-up for diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: Legg-Calve-Perthes, not SCFE. Once again, it’s on the NBME exam, so if you think it’s weird or disagree, don’t take it up with me;

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + sickle cell disease + painful hip pain and limp; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: “avascular necrosis”; Legg-Calve-Perthes is wrong answer; remember that LCP is idiopathic avascular necrosis; if the cause is known (i.e., sickle cell, Gaucher, corticosteroids), LCP is wrong.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + hepatomegaly + hip pain + macrophages with wrinkled tissue appearance; Q asks mechanism for disorder
rapidFireQAs.a: deficiency of glucocerebrosidase; diagnosis is Gaucher disease; for Gaucher, you just need to know it’s the answer if you get a glycogen storage disease + a bone problem.

rapidFireQAs.q: 9F + painful left hip + x-ray shows no abnormalities + diagnosis is made using bone-scan; Q just asks the most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: Legg-Calve-Perthes; x-ray can be negative initially; in this case, the next best step is bone-scan or MRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: 7F + hip pain + x-ray is shown below; Q asks for diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: Legg-Calve-Perthes; student says, “No idea what I’m looking at.” Relax. If we try to imagine, the right femoral head (left side of image) looks “contracted” or “flattened.” Once again, this is HY and buzzy for avascular necrosis. You can still answer this without the x-ray since the hip diagnosis in a kid 5-8 is almost always LCP anyway.

rapidFireQAs.q: 59F + advanced rheumatoid arthritis managed with multiple medications + MRI of pelvis is shown; Q wants diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: avascular necrosis; etiology is chronic corticosteroids in the setting of advanced autoimmune disease; the right femoral head (left side of image) appears hypointense (more black). The necrotic / lack of bone in the black superior portion of the femoral head means the remaining white part of the femoral head is “flattened” or “contracted.” The left femoral head (right side of image) shows a small area of necrosis as well (black medial portion). Regardless, you don't even need to know what you're looking at, because the stem telling you it's a patient with autoimmune disease taking multiple meds should scream avascular necrosis due to prednisone use anyway.

rapidFireQAs.q: 13M + left hip pain + walks with antalgic gait + 95%tile for weight; Q asks mechanism for patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: “displacement of the epiphysis of the femoral head”; diagnosis is SCFE; classic vignette is overweight pre-adolescent boy with a painful limp; “antalgic gait” just means walking with a painful limp; it is non-specific and I’ve seen this descriptor used in LCP vignettes as well.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + left hip pain + BMI 20 + 6’0” + x-ray is shown below; Q asks diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: slipped capital femoral epiphysis; x-ray shows the “ice cream slipping off its cone”; student is confused because the Q says BMI is normal; as I said earlier, although the kid being overweight is HY and buzzy, plenty of NBME Qs either don’t mention the BMI or will say it’s normal; it’s the age that matters (i.e., 10-13).

rapidFireQAs.q: “Do I need to know the mechanism of PTH on bone?” → Yes, it’s HY.
rapidFireQAs.a: PTH binds to osteoblasts, not -clasts. This sounds paradoxical, since osteoblasts build bone and PTH has the role of causing bone resorption in order to increase serum calcium. After PTH binds to the osteoblast, it will express RANK-ligand (RANK-L) on its cell surface. RANK-L then binds to RANK receptor on osteoclasts, which in turn resorb (break down) the bone.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about OPG in relation to RANK-L. Can you quickly clarify.”
rapidFireQAs.a: Osteoprotegerin (OPG) is protective of bone loss. It is a RANK receptor decoy (i.e., it looks like RANK receptor), and therefore acts as an endogenous competitive inhibitor of RANK-L. In other words, if more OPG is present, then RANK-L will bind to OPG instead of RANK receptor, thereby resulting in less osteoclast activation and less bone resorption. OPG is suppressed by cytokines (namely IL-1). Therefore, too much cytokine activity can cause osteoporosis. In fact, IL-1 is also known as osteoclast-activating factor. Estrogen suppresses cytokine activity (IL-1) on bone, resulting in an increased OPG/RANK-L ratio and lower risk of bone resorption. In post-menopausal state, ↓ estrogen → ↓ suppression of IL-1 on bone → ↓ OPG/RANK-L ratio → ↑ bone resorption → osteoporosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and bone?”
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants you to know that increased osteoblast activity causes high ALP. This is why ALP levels go up when PTH is high, or why ALP is elevated in Paget disease of bone. There is Q on one of the Step 1 NBMEs where they give weird craniofacial syndrome + low serum ALP; they ask what cell is defective → answer = osteoblast; students have freaked out to me over this Q (“we need to know this crazy/weird syndrome??”) → No. The syndrome is irrelevant. The Q says low ALP, so they just want the osteoblast as the cell that’s impaired. HY Bone density/architectural conditions

rapidFireQAs.q: 62F + shows graph with lines of bone density for two different women without family history of osteoporosis; Q asks what is the reason why one woman has higher bone density than the other
rapidFireQAs.a: ethnicity; black race is protective against osteoporosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 64F + image of vertebral column shown below; Q asks what is responsible for this patient’s condition:
rapidFireQAs.a: Interleukin-1; IL-1 is aka osteoclast-activating factor; post-menopausal state → ↓ estrogen → ↓ suppression of cytokines (namely IL-1) on bone → ↓ OPG/RANK-L ratio → bone resorption → osteoporosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + runs a lot + BMI 20 + no other issues; Q asks what patient is at increased risk for
rapidFireQAs.a: osteoporosis; makes no sense, as BMI isn’t low, but

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + bitemporal hemianopsia + 20-lb weight gain past 6 months + compression fracture of a vertebra; Q asks what the tumor is secreting
rapidFireQAs.a: ACTH; patient has Cushing disease; cortisol can cause osteoporosis; compression fractures = osteoporosis on USMLE; student asks, “But why can’t TSH be the answer? Can’t hyperthyroidism cause osteoporosis?” → Two points: 1) Patient here has weight gain, not weight loss. If patient has hyperthyroidism, we wouldn’t have weight gain; 2) Despite this notion that hyperthyroidism could in theory cause osteoporosis, I’ve never seen that assessed on NBME material.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72F + fractures femur + no mention of osteoporosis; Q asks, during the rehabilitation process, what is the most important predictor of success in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: “activity level before the fracture” → protective of bone density / osteoporosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4M + came to USA from Ireland with parents one year ago + has bowed tibias; Q asks serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH
rapidFireQAs.a: low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH; diagnosis is rickets with genu varum.

rapidFireQAs.q: 70F + type II diabetes + renal failure + left hip pain; Q asks most likely MSK diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: osteomalacia; renal failure causes low vitamin D, resulting in osteomalacia; renal osteodystrophy = osteomalacia cause by renal failure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 70F + renal failure + left hip pain + x-ray shows pseudofracture; Q asks what’s most likely responsible for this patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: “decreased intestinal absorption of calcium”; we have osteomalacia due to low 1,25-D3, causing reduced intestinal absorption. “Pseudofracture” is buzzy for osteomalacia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 70F + left hip pain + x-ray shows pseudofracture; Q asks arrows for calcium, phosphate, PTH, and calcitriol
rapidFireQAs.a: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH, low calcitriol (aka 1,25-D3); even though vitamin D is low, phosphate is always high in renal failure; so even though, yes, vitamin D deficiency causes low calcium and low phosphate in the setting of rickets/osteomalacia, if the patient has renal failure, the renal failure “wins” when it comes to phosphate. Exceedingly HY.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + recurrent fractures + increased bone density; Q asks which type of molecular signaling is up
rapidFireQAs.a: GM-CSF; diagnosis is osteopetrosis, which is caused by either deficiency of carbonic anhydrase II, or a problem with GM-CSF signaling; osteoclasts are defective.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + recurrent fractures + engages well with the parents + mom has history of recurrent miscarriages; Q asks mechanism for patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: “defect of procollagen synthesis”; diagnosis is osteogenesis imperfecta (collagen I gene mutation); USMLE doesn’t actually care about the exact collagen step that is defective; the answer will be the only one that refers to collagen.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + falls off bike while BMX dirt jumping + broken radius + cast applied + now has acutely increased severe pain in arm; Q asks for most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: compartment syndrome; although circumferential burns are fixated on as hyper-HY for compartment syndrome on USMLE, it’s to my observation NBME cares less about this and more about acute casting as the highest yield cause. If a limb is placed in a cast before swelling has maximized, compartment syndrome can result, where the patient experiences increasingly severe pain and paresthesias of the limb.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20M + housefire + 3rd -degree burns all over legs + severe pain in left leg; Q asks for next best step
rapidFireQAs.a: “measure compartment pressures”; treatment is then “fasciotomy.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + central chest pain + worsens when reaches behind her back and over her head + pain on palpation; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: costochondritis; any chest pain on USMLE that worsens with change in positioning (except pericarditis, which worsens when leaning back), think MSK etiology – i.e., costochondritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + pain in chest + worse when reaching behind her back and over her head + there is no pain on palpation; Q wants treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAIDs; diagnosis is costochondritis. I’ve seen NBME Qs where they mention pain that changes with position and/or with palpation – i.e., it need not be both.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + recently recovered from viral infection + severe right lateral chest pain + no friction rub + increased serum creatine kinase; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: pleurodynia. Despite the name, this has nothing to do with the lungs/pleura. It is intercostal muscle spasm following viral infection (i.e., viral myalgia) that presents as lateral chest pain; CK can be elevated due to increased muscle tone.

rapidFireQAs.q: 47M + alcoholic + found on bench in park + urine dipstick shows 2+ blood + urine RBCs negative; Q wants most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: rhabdomyolysis; alcoholism is huge risk factor; urinalysis classically shows false-positive blood on dipstick, where the dipstick can’t differentiate between free myoglobin and RBC hemoglobin, but light microscopy will be negative.

rapidFireQAs.q: 47M + alcoholic + found on bench in park + serum potassium elevated + urine shows brown pigmented casts; Q wants most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: rhabdomyolysis; urine can be either false- positive blood on dipstick or characteristic of acute tubular necrosis (i.e., brown pigmented casts, or dirty/muddy brown granular casts).

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about bone tumors?
rapidFireQAs.a: ” HY bone tumor points for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: 1-year-old boy + leukocoria (white pupil) + Q wants to know what he is most likely to develop later in life
rapidFireQAs.a: osteosarcoma; diagnosis is congenital retinoblastoma; Rb mutations cause both retinoblastoma as well as osteosarcoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20M + pain in left distal femur + x-ray shows elevation of periosteum and spiculated new bone formation; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: osteosarcoma; elevation of periosteum = Codman triangle; spiculated new bone formation = sunburst appearance.

rapidFireQAs.q: 61M + pain in left hip + histo image below; Q just asks for diagnosis straight-up:
rapidFireQAs.a: chondrosarcoma; easy if you know this HY image.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + pain in right hip + x-ray shows tumor + biopsy shows glistening / shiny lesion; Q wants to know what is most likely to be characteristic of this lesion
rapidFireQAs.a: “chondrocytes embedded in lacunae”; diagnosis is chondrosacoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + pain in proximal tibia + x-ray shows a lesion + pain is relieved with ibuprofen; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: osteoid osteoma; this is the answer on USMLE if they give a bone tumor where the pain is relieved with NSAIDs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + 1-cm hard mass growing from skull + father died of colon cancer at age 32; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: Gardner syndrome presenting with osteoma. Gardner syndrome = familial adenomatous polyposis + either osteoma or lipoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + fever 101 F + pain in left forearm + bone scan shows uptake in the diaphysis; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: Ewing sarcoma; can present similarly to osteomyelitis, except bone scan is more likely to show uptake in the diaphysis; in osteomyelitis, the uptake is in the metaphysis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + fever 101 F + pain in left forearm + biopsy with histo image of lesion shown below; Q asks for the genetics:
rapidFireQAs.a: t(11;22) translocation; diagnosis is Ewing sarcoma; image shows the small blue cells of neuroendocrine origin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + pain in upper left humerus + x-ray shown below; Q wants diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: unicameral bone cyst. This is an underrated diagnosis for USMLE but shows up on the real deal.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37M + pain in right elbow + x-ray is shown below; Q asks diagnosis (answers are all bone tumors):
rapidFireQAs.a: giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma); x-ray shows soap-bubble appearance. In contrast to unicameral bone cyst, which occurs usually from birth to age 20, osteoclastoma usually occurs age 20-40.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M + diffuse bone pain + high serum calcium; bone scan is shown below; Q wants diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: metastatic malignancy (most likely prostate cancer if no past medical history); wrong answer is primary hyperparathyroidism; metastases are important cause of high Ca2+ .

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + large, yellow, soft infiltrating mass in gluteus maximus + biopsy shows irregular vacuolated cells + clear cells with many mitoses; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: liposarcoma; lipoma is wrong answer (presumably would sound less sinister / not invasive, clearly); lipoma = benign tumor of fat (Gardner syndrome); liposarcoma = malignant tumor of fat; rhabdomyoma = benign tumor of striated (skeletal or cardiac) muscle (usually tuberous sclerosis with cardiac rhabdomyoma); rhabdomyosarcoma = malignant tumor of striated muscle (usually sarcoma botryoides in pediatrics).

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about fracture types for USMLE?”
rapidFireQAs.a: I’ll give summary here: HY bone fracture points for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + car accident + linear skull fracture; Q asks what type of bleed is most likely in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: epidural hematoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20M + car accident + high blood pressure + bradycardia + bruising around the eyes and behind the ears + low GCS score; Q asks for most likely reason for the patient’s high blood pressure
rapidFireQAs.a: increased intracranial pressure; Cushing reflex = triad of HTN + bradycardia + bradypnea due to increased ICP; patient here has base of skull fracture (Battle sign + raccoon eyes); Q need not mention all four findings (i.e., rhinorrhea + otorrhea as well).

rapidFireQAs.q: 37M + cyclist + mild weakness of finger abduction/adduction + has positive Froment sign; Q asks which structure is most likely compressed
rapidFireQAs.a: “deep branch of ulnar nerve at the hook of hamate.”

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about myopathy / muscular dystrophies for USMLE?
rapidFireQAs.a: ” HY myopathies / muscular dystrophies for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR); presents as pain and stiffness of proximal muscles, usually in patient over 50; Q will not mention anything about elevated CK or weakness on physical exam.

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR and CK; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: polymyositis, not PMR, because Q mentions CK elevation. Pain and stiffness are not unique to PMR. They can absolutely be seen in polymyositis. The notion that they are unique to PMR is complete nonsense for USMLE purposes.

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR + normal CK + physical exam shows 3/5 strength in shoulders; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: polymyositis; even though CK is normal, patient has weakness on physical exam.

rapidFireQAs.q: 64F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR + weakness on physical exam; Q wants next best step in diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: “electromyography and nerve conduction studies”; diagnosis is polymyositis; Q will not force you to choose between anti-Jo1 antibodies and EMG/NCS, but the latter is correct on NBME forms; biopsy is confirmatory.

rapidFireQAs.q: 64F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + physical exam shows weakness + anti-Jo1 antibodies are positive; Q asks the most likely pathophysiology for this patient’s condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: “CD8 + T cells and macrophages surrounding muscle fibers.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 64F + bilateral temporal headache + slightly blurry vision on left + high ESR + bilateral hip pain; Q wants next best step
rapidFireQAs.a: “IV methylprednisolone”; temporal (giant cell) arteritis can show up bilaterally on NBME forms; do steroids first to prevent blindness, then do biopsy of temporal artery; the patient’s hip pain is polymyalgia rheumatica, which is linked with temporal arteritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 64F + right-sided temporal pain + high ESR + low-grade fever + pain in the jaw + low hemoglobin; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: giant cell arteritis; can present with jaw claudication; low hemoglobin is due to anemia of chronic disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: 64F + right-sided temporal and facial pain + worsens with eating + proximal muscles a little stiff; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: temporomandibular joint dysfunction, not temporal arteritis; if it worsens with eating, then they want TMJ dysfunction, not jaw claudication.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + 6-month history of muscle pain; physical exam shows 12 symmetric tender points; ESR not elevated; Q wants treatment
rapidFireQAs.a: “anti-depressant therapy”; diagnosis is fibromyalgia; this is a psych condition treated with SSRIs; as mentioned earlier, students get confused here because the patient is not depressed, but SSRIs are still anti-depressant medication.

rapidFireQAs.q: 61F + 20-pound weight loss past one month despite no change in diet + fatigue + anemia + proximal muscle weakness + increased serum CK + pulling sensation in groin + Q shows image below; Q wants to know diagnosis (all cancers listed):
rapidFireQAs.a: ovarian adenocarcinoma; for whatever magical reason, dermatomyositis can be a paraneoplastic syndrome of ovarian cancer. Around 10-20% of women with dermatomyositis have ovarian cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + 6-month history of low energy and fatigue + gradually lengthening periods + HR 60 + hepatic AST, total cholesterol, and serum creatine kinase are elevated; Q asks most likely diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: hypothyroidism (Hashimoto); elevated CK is due to hypothyroid myopathy, which may or may not present with proximal muscle weakness in the vignette; transaminases can be elevated in thyroid dysfunction; USMLE likes menstrual irregularities, bradycardia, high cholesterol, dysthymia, doughy skin, and carpal tunnel syndrome in hypothyroidism. Details such as cold intolerance, weight gain, brittle hair, and constipation are often omitted because they’re too easy/buzzy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 66M + started taking a statin and fibrate simultaneously + develops myopathy; Q wants mechanism
rapidFireQAs.a: “P-450-mediated interaction.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + hypotonia + lactic acidosis + no mention of eye/ear problems + biopsy of muscle shows ragged red fibers; Q wants most likely inheritance
rapidFireQAs.a: mitochondrial.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + large calves + uses arms to walk up off the floor; Q wants organelle / cellular structure that is disrupted in patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: cytoskeleton; a-/b-dystroglycan are encoded by the DMD (dystrophin) gene and are required for proper anchoring of the muscle cell cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + large calves + uses arms to walk up off the floor + Q wants to know what will be seen on muscle biopsy
rapidFireQAs.a: “connective tissue stromal cells” or “fibroadipose tissue”; patient will have pseudohypertrophy, which is replacement of muscle cells with connective tissue.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + large calves + uses arms to walk up off the floor; Q wants molecular mechanism for patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: frameshift mutation; this results in truncated, non-functional protein due to early formation of stop codon.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18M + increasing muscle weakness and muscular enlargement + maternal uncle died of cardiomyopathy in his 20s; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: Becker muscular dystrophy; less severe form of Duchenne; usually due to non-frameshift mutations in the DMD gene. Becker usually presents in adolescence or young adulthood; Duchenne will be a kid.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4M + short arms and legs; trunk and head are normal size; parents are normal; Q wants mechanism for patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: gonadal (germline) mosaicism; diagnosis is achondroplasia; disease is constitutive activation of FGFR3 gene; results in failed cartilage conversion into bone; presents as shortened limbs but normal head size and postural height (trunk size); condition is autosomal dominant, but both parents will usually be of normal height, which means the original mutation occurred in a gonadal cell (usually a spermatogonium of the father), where the child has 100% of cells affected as a result, despite the father being unaffected. I also talk about this stuff in more detail in my HY Biochem PDF.

rapidFireQAs.q: “How HY is hernia stuff for USMLE?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Unfortunately decently HY. But good news: I’ll tell you exactly what you need to know for them for USMLE without all of the absolute nonsense. HY MSK hernia points for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: 1-year-old boy + enlarged testis + scrotal mass that is reducible with pressure over deep inguinal ring; Q asks mechanism for patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: patent processus vaginalis; diagnosis is indirect inguinal hernia; mechanism is same as formation of hydrocele; since the hernia passes through deep inguinal ring (which is lateral to inferior epigastric artery), pressure applied to the ring can reduce the hernia. With direct inguinal hernia, in contrast, since it does not pass through the deep inguinal ring, this examination maneuver wil not reduce the hernia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12-year-old boy + testicular mass that enlarges with cough and reduces when lying down; pressure applied over deep inguinal ring hides hernia; Q wants to know whether the hernia is lateral vs medial to inferior epigastric artery, and whether it’s inferior or superior to inguinal ligament
rapidFireQAs.a: lateral to inferior epigastric artery + superior to inguinal ligament; diagnosis is indirect inguinal hernia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 64M + bulging mass in groin + not painful; worsens with cough and improves when supine; Q wants location of hernia relative to inferior epigastric artery
rapidFireQAs.a: medial to inferior epigastric artery; diagnosis is direct inguinal hernia; usually occurs in older men.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + pain and palpable mass in groin inferior to inguinal ligament; Q wants to know which structure is lateral to the mass
rapidFireQAs.a: femoral vein; diagnosis is femoral hernia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 60M + Q shows CT scan of an abnormality with arrow pointing to it; asks for what the medial border of the hernia is (in other words, what is medial to the arrow)?
rapidFireQAs.a: lateral border of rectus abdominus; diagnosis is Spigelian hernia; hernia protrudes just lateral to the linea semilunaris. Students get hysterical and worried when they see CT scans like this. Recognize that the USMLE doesn’t care that you even know what a Spigelian hernia is in order to get this question right. If you chill out for a second and try to imagine what you’re looking at in the CT, you can tell the rectus abdominis is at the superior part of the image, which means the hernia is just lateral to it.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M + pelvic hernia + physical exam causes worsening of pain when ipsilateral leg is extended, medially rotated, and abducted; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: obturator hernia; the Howship- Romberg sign is used to diagnose. The USMLE can be vague with this question, where they just tell you “patient has hernia that’s worsened with this exam maneuver” and you have to know it’s obturator hernia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8-month-old boy + large tongue + hypotonia + umbilical hernia; Q asks what would have most likely prevented this patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: routine newborn screening; diagnosis is congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism); heel-prick test at birth tests for hypothyroidism, PKU, and galactose disorders, among others.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonatal male + enlarged occiput + clenched fingers + rocker-bottom feet + protrusion of abdominal contents through umbilicus that are covered in thin membrane; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: trisomy 18 (Edward syndrome); omphalocele is described; in contrast, gastroschisis protrudes to the right of the umbilicus and is not covered in a layer of peritoneal membrane.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Is there any chest wall MSK I should know?”
rapidFireQAs.a: For a thoracentesis (removing fluid from the pleural space when treating a pleural effusion) or needle decompression (for pneumothorax), the needle should be inserted just above the rib. This is in order to avoid injury to the neurovascular bundle that sits at the inferior margin of each rib. For an intercostal nerve block, however, we want to anesthetize the nerve, so the needle should be inserted just below each rib (i.e., at the inferior margin). 40M + car accident + severe, left-sided chest pain; Q asks, the most likely pathway of this patient’s chest pain is carried by which nerve → answer = intercostal. The numerical rib location for needle insertion for a thoracentesis varies depending on the source (i.e., literature says 8-10th ribs), but offline NBME has Q where answer is midaxillary line above the 9th rib. When performing a needle decompression followed by chest tube for pneumothorax, the typical location for insertion is the second intercostal space (just superior to the third rib).

rapidFireQAs.q: “Is there any high-yield neck anatomy I should know?
rapidFireQAs.a: ” HY neck MSK masses for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: “Do I need to know nasal sinus/concha anatomy for USMLE?
rapidFireQAs.a: There are rare Qs that show up asking sinus anatomy, but now that Step 1 is P/F, I’d say studying this is largely venturing into left-field territory. There is a question on one of the offline Step 1 NBMEs, however, where they say there is a sinus infection with purulent discharge coming from the sphenoethmoid recess, and they ask for the location of this structure → answer = “superior to the superior concha.” You can memorize this one point, but as I said, I don’t think you need to be sitting in your room obsessing over nasal anatomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Are there any random HY points for pediatrics I should know?”
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE likes bone age in some vignettes. If an x-ray is done of the hand, the approximate age of the child can be ascertained; if the child is short and “bone age equals chronologic age,” that is genuine short stature (e.g., familial short stature; I’ve also seen this in Turner syndrome Qs); if the child is short and “bone age is less than chronologic age,” then the answer is “constitutional short stature,” or “constitutional growth delay,” which means the child’s growth curve is merely shifted to the right but he/she will catch up (i.e., boy is 4’11” in 9th grade but will eventually become average height); the Q will often say the parents are average height; if they don’t mention bone age for constitutional short stature Qs, they can say the child is Tanner stage 1 or 2 (prepubescent). If child abuse is suspected, sometimes the answer can be “obtain skeletal survey” in order to evaluate for radiographic evidence of fractures at different stages of healing.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Anything I should know about random infections and muscle?”
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE likes myalgias = influenza virus when patient has head cold. Vignette will be big paragraph + they mention muscle pain in there + answers are all different viruses; answer is simply influenza. Taenia solium (pork tapeworm; pork cestode) can cause cysts in muscle (myalgia). Trichinella spiralis (pork roundworm; pork nematode) can cause triad of fever + periorbital edema + myalgias in patient who recently ate pork or bear meat.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Anything I should know about random immuno and MSK?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Muscle pain at the site of injection of a drug or vaccine 3-7 days post-injection = Arthus reaction = type III hypersensitivity (immune complexes); was seen with Moderna Covid vaccine (“Moderna arm”). Polyarthritis 3-7 days following injection of a drug = serum sickness = type III hypersensitivity (immune complexes). USMLE will give you image of malar rash of lupus (type III hypersensitivity) and then ask which condition is most similar → answer = Arthus reaction, or serum sickness, or PSGN.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Anything random I should know about genetics and MSK?”
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants you to know the Hox genes, or homeobox genes, are necessary for proper body/limb patterning (i.e., body parts developing at correct locations). They will say if Hox genes 9-12 are turned on, phalanges are produced; when only 9-11 are turned on, carpal bones are produced. Q asks, “why did carpal bones develop instead of phalanges?” → answer = 12 not turned on. Not hard, but I’ve seen this confuse students. Newborn dies shortly after birth + autopsy shows transformation of lumbar vertebrae into thoracic vertebrae; Q wants mechanism → answer = “inappropriate expression of Hox genes normally transcribed cranially.” Cranially = toward the head; caudally = toward the “tail.”

rapidFireQAs.q: “Is there any HY Pharm I should know in relation to MSK?
rapidFireQAs.a: ” Highest yield “MSK pharm” for USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: Identify the diagnosis & key pearl (MSK & Anatomy Vignette):
rapidFireQAs.a: 32F + history of multiple sclerosis with muscular spasticity; Q asks the mechanism of action of the drug used to treat her spasticity → answer = GABAB receptor agonist; drug is baclofen. 45M + started on aripiprazole for schizophrenia + develops stiff neck; Q wants mechanism of action of treatment → answer = anti-muscarinic (anti-cholinergic); diagnosis is acute dystonia due to anti-psychotic use; treatment for acute dystonia is either benztropine (muscarinic receptor antagonist), OR diphenhydramine or chlorpheniramine (both first- generation H1 receptor antagonists); any of these three drugs can show up as the answer on USMLE. The 1st -gen H1 blockers have nasty anti-cholinergic side-effects, but that’s actually a good thing when we want to treat acute dystonia. 45M + started on antipsychotic + develop muscle rigidity + fever of 103 F; Q wants mechanism of action of treatment → answer = “inhibition of intracellular calcium release”; diagnosis is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS); treatment is dantrolene. 45M + started on antipsychotic + develop muscle rigidity + temperature is 98.6 F; Q wants mechanism of action of treatment → answer = anti-muscarinic (anti-cholinergic); drug is either benztropine (muscarinic receptor antagonist) or a 1st -gen H1 blocker (anti-cholinergic side-effects that are actually good for Tx); diagnosis is acute dystonia, not neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS); if the Q wants NMS, they’ll give muscle rigidity + fever; in contrast, muscle rigidity + no fever = acute dystonia. 52F + undergoes surgery + develops high fever and muscle rigidity; Q asks what drug most likely caused this patient’s condition → answer = succinylcholine, a nicotinic receptor antagonist that enables paralysis during surgery. It is known as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Diagnosis is malignant hyperthermia, which has same mechanism as NMS, except it is classically caused by succinylcholine, not antipsychotics. Malignant hyperthermia is treated with dantrolene, same as with NMS. 52F + undergoes surgery with general anesthesia + receives vecuronium; Q just wants mechanism of action → answer = nicotinic receptor antagonist; drugs such as vecuronium and rocuronium are non-depolarizing neuromuscular junction blockers. In contrast, succinylcholine is a depolarizing blocker. HY ANATOMY/MSK/RHEUM

rapidFireQAs.q: Waiter tip position in kid
rapidFireQAs.a: upper brachial plexus injury → C5/6 → Erb-Duchenne palsy

rapidFireQAs.q: Claw hand
rapidFireQAs.a: lower brachial plexus → C8/T1 → Klumpke palsy

rapidFireQAs.q: Pronated arm + wrist-drop
rapidFireQAs.a: radial nerve injury

rapidFireQAs.q: Midshaft fracture of humerus
rapidFireQAs.a: Radial nerve injury

rapidFireQAs.q: Supracondylar fracture of humerus
rapidFireQAs.a: median nerve injury

rapidFireQAs.q: Surgical neck of humerus fracture
rapidFireQAs.a: axillary nerve injury

rapidFireQAs.q: Medial epicondylar injury
rapidFireQAs.a: ulnar nerve injury

rapidFireQAs.q: Point tenderness over a vertebra in older woman
rapidFireQAs.a: osteoporosis (compression fracture)

rapidFireQAs.q: Point tenderness over a vertebra in younger patient on steroids
rapidFireQAs.a: osteoporosis (compression fracture)

rapidFireQAs.q: Point tenderness over a vertebra in patient with autoimmune disease
rapidFireQAs.a: recognize patient is on steroids → osteoporosis (compression fracture)

rapidFireQAs.q: Back pain worse in the morning and gets better throughout day in male 20s-40s
rapidFireQAs.a: ankylosing spondylitis

rapidFireQAs.q: Bamboo spine
rapidFireQAs.a: ankylosing spondylitis

rapidFireQAs.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
rapidFireQAs.a: atlantoaxial subluxation

rapidFireQAs.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
rapidFireQAs.a: MR of spine to Dx atlantoaxial subluxation

rapidFireQAs.q: Prior to surgery in rheumatoid arthritis patient
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical CT or flexion/extension x-rays of cervical spine to check for atlantoaxial subluxation

rapidFireQAs.q: Heart problem in neonate of mom with SLE
rapidFireQAs.a: congenital third-degree heartblock

rapidFireQAs.q: Infective causes of third-degree
rapidFireQAs.a: Lyme disease, congenital lupus, diphtheria

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of anemia of chronic disease if renal failure not cause (IBD, RA, SLE, etc.)
rapidFireQAs.a: CANNOT give EPO; Tx underlying condition.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of acute gout
rapidFireQAs.a: indomethacin (NSAID) first on USMLE; then steroids, then colchicine

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of acute gout if indomethacin + steroids not listed
rapidFireQAs.a: colchicine

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of acute gout in pt with renal insufficiency or Hx of renal transplant
rapidFireQAs.a: steroids

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of chronic gout (decrease recurrence)
rapidFireQAs.a: allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors)

rapidFireQAs.q: Crystal type in pseudogout
rapidFireQAs.a: calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

rapidFireQAs.q: Same male + painful hands + x-ray shows DIP involvement. Joint pain Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudogout

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of pseudogout
rapidFireQAs.a: same as gout acutely; Tx underlying condition for chronic

rapidFireQAs.q: Biggest risk factor for osteoarthritis
rapidFireQAs.a: obesity

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of osteoarthritis
rapidFireQAs.a: weight loss; if normal BMI → acetaminophen before NSAIDs

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with OA taking naproxen (NSAID) + peripheral edema
rapidFireQAs.a: increased renal retention of sodium

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of rheumatoid arthritis
