rapidFireQAs.a: Two-armed: symptom-relief + disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs)

rapidFireQAs.q: Symptom-relief for RA
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAID first, then steroids (these do symptoms only; do not slow disease progression)

rapidFireQAs.q: DMARDs for early RA
rapidFireQAs.a: always methotrexate first; if insufficient, add another DMARD (sulfasalazine or leflunomide); if insufficient add anti-TNF-alpha agent

rapidFireQAs.q: Sulfasalazine MOA
rapidFireQAs.a: metabolized into sulfapyridine + mesalamine in the gut by bacteria Mesalamine is 5-ASA absorbed as the Tx for RA; only NSAID considered to be DMARD

rapidFireQAs.q: Most specific Abs in RA
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptide), not RF (rheumatoid factor)

rapidFireQAs.q: X-ray of hands in RA vs OA
rapidFireQAs.a: Only OA has DIPs involved; RA is PIPs + MCPs

rapidFireQAs.q: Symmetry in RA vs OA
rapidFireQAs.a: RA is symmetrical; OA is not

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt groups most likely to get SA
rapidFireQAs.a: prosthetic joints, RA/OA, recent intense exercise/joint trauma; peds (JRA)

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt with OA or RA has red, warm, tender knee
rapidFireQAs.a: do arthrocentesis (septic arthritis)

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid + recurrent knee redness, warmth, pain + fever
rapidFireQAs.a: Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA; Still disease)

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common presentation finding in SLE
rapidFireQAs.a: arthritis (>90%)

rapidFireQAs.q: Woman 20s-40s + arthritis + thrombocytopenia
rapidFireQAs.a: SLE

rapidFireQAs.q: Woman 20s-40s + arthritis + mouth ulcer + circular skin lesions
rapidFireQAs.a: SLE

rapidFireQAs.q: Malar rash + low RBCs + low WBCs + low platelets; mechanism for low cell lines?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased peripheral destruction (antibodies against hematologic cells lines seen in SLE; isolated thrombocytopenia most common)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of SLE flare
rapidFireQAs.a: steroids

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of lupus nephritis
rapidFireQAs.a: mycophenolate mofetil

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of discoid lupus
rapidFireQAs.a: hydroxychloroquine

rapidFireQAs.q: Most specific Abs for SLE
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-Smith (RNP), not anti-dsDNA

rapidFireQAs.q: Which Abs go up in acute SLE flares
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-dsDNA (and C3 goes down)

rapidFireQAs.q: Drug-induced lupus Abs
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-histone

rapidFireQAs.q: Viral-induced aplastic anemia; mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: defective bone marrow production (contrast with SLE)

rapidFireQAs.q: IBD + eczematoid plaque on forehead + sore joints
rapidFireQAs.a: psoriatic arthritis (HLA-B27 → PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis)

rapidFireQAs.q: IBD + back pain
rapidFireQAs.a: sacroiliitis (or ankylosing spondylitis)

rapidFireQAs.q: What kind of vignette is a patient classically on naproxen?
rapidFireQAs.a: osteoarthritis (OA).

rapidFireQAs.q: How do we treat OA?
rapidFireQAs.a: weight loss (biggest risk factor is obesity), then acetaminophen, then NSAIDs → sometimes USMLE will mention naproxen being taken by OA patient to illustrate this common scenario of poor self-management → acetaminophen recommended before NSAIDs because the renal damage caused by NSAID use.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + unilateral temporal headache + blurry vision; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: temporal arteritis

rapidFireQAs.q: What other condition is TA associated with?
rapidFireQAs.a: polymyalgia rheumatica (in fact, they’re considered to be on the same disease spectrum, rather than as two inherently distinct conditions)

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + unilateral temporal headache + muscle pain/stiffness
rapidFireQAs.a: temporal arteritis + polymyalgia rheumatica

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for PR if patient doesn’t also have temporal arteritis
rapidFireQAs.a: oral steroids are okay bc not an emergency.

rapidFireQAs.q: Polymyalgia rheumatica vs polymyositis
rapidFireQAs.a: PR presents with stiffness/pain generally without weakness; polymyositis can present with pain, but it also has proximal muscle weakness. Both conditions can present with elevations of ESR and CRP, so these aren’t reliable for Dx.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of polymyositis
rapidFireQAs.a: same as with dermatomyositis, do anti-Jo1 and -Mi2 antibodies, then do confirmatory muscle biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Violaceous rash around the eyelids
rapidFireQAs.a: heliotrope rash → Dx = dermatomyositis (don’t confuse that with malar rash of SLE).

rapidFireQAs.q: Rash around back of neck + top of back + adult with proximal muscle weakness (difficulty standing from chair unassisted)
rapidFireQAs.a: shawl rash → dermatomyositis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of dermatomyositis
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-Jo1 or -Mi2 antibodies first → muscle biopsy confirmatory.

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE wants you to know that in dermatomyositis, there’s specifically an increased risk of what?
rapidFireQAs.a: malignancy (non-Hodgkin lymphoma) → that being said, autoimmune diseases in general increase the risk of NHL → so if you have, e.g., patient with SLE with irregular ring-enhancing lesion on head CT, answer = primary CNS lymphoma, not toxoplasmosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for flare of polymyositis/dermatomyositis
rapidFireQAs.a: oral corticosteroids.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + arthritis + mouth ulcer + low platelets; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: SLE

rapidFireQAs.q: First Tx for carpal tunnel syndrome in patient who can’t stop offending activity (e.g., office worker)
rapidFireQAs.a: wrist splint first; then triamcinolone (steroid) injection into the carpal tunnel; do not select anything surgical as it’s always wrong on the USMLE; NSAIDs are a wrong answer and not proven to help

rapidFireQAs.q: What is cubital tunnel syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at elbow → presents similarly to carpal tunnel syndrome but just in an ulnar distribution and involves the forearm.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is Guyon canal syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist → hook of hamate fracture or chronic handle bar impaction in avid cyclists.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43M + elevated fasting glucose + arthritis + cardiomegaly; what’s the mechanism for this patient’s condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased intestinal absorption of iron; Dx = hemochromatosis; AR; chromosome 6; Fe can deposit in tail of pancreas, leading to diabetes; hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism are two HY causes of pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease); this will carry an osteoarthritis-like presentation (i.e., even with findings such as Heberden nodes), but the vignette will be hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism, so you know the Dx is pseudogout; Fe can deposit in the heart, leading to either dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy; Fe can deposit in the hypothalamus and/or testes, causing infertility; “Bronze diabetes” = hyperpigmentation of the skin due to hemosiderin deposition → e.g., patient with darkening of the skin of the forearms, increased fasting glucose, and infertility or arthritis; answer = “check serum iron and ferritin.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + rheumatoid arthritis + currently being managed with infliximab but has not improved; Q asks for which immune mediator is most likely contributing to symptoms; answer = IL-1. Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody against soluble TNFa (not TNFa receptor); even though TNFa plays a role in rheumatoid arthritis, we know TNFa is not the answer here because the patient is already on a med for it; IL-1 and IL-6 are cytokines known to cause inflammation in RA; tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody against IL-6 receptor that can be used for advanced RA.
rapidFireQAs.a: Normal Tx for RA is two-armed: symptoms and DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs). For Sx: USMLE wants NSAIDs followed by steroids; these do not slow disease progression. For slowing disease progression, the first-line DMARD is almost always methotrexate. If this fails or patient has contraindications to it (i.e., pulmonary or hepatic disease), use an anti- TNFa drug.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + rheumatoid arthritis + PR-depressions and ST-elevations seen in many leads on ECG; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: pericarditis; common in autoimmune diseases such as RA; PR-depressions are highly specific for pericarditis but not common; diffuse ST-elevations seen in all cases on USMLE if they mention ECG findings.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient has autoimmune disease (i.e., SLE, RA, etc.); question wants to know how to decrease recurrence of flares
rapidFireQAs.a: smoking cessation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + long-standing history of rheumatoid arthritis managed with prednisone + undergoes appendectomy + experiences drop of BP to 80/40 during surgery; risk factor for this precipitous drop in BP?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic prednisone use causing adrenal suppression → can’t mount stress response in setting of stressor (i.e., surgery, trauma, infection) → can cause BP to fall precipitously → after IV fluids, give hydrocortisone. Normally, cortisol (i.e., glucocorticoid) from the adrenals helps maintain BP by upregulating alpha-1 receptors on arterioles; NE and E (catecholamines) agonize alpha-1 to maintain BP; this is called permissive effects of glucocorticoids on catecholamines. Patients with suppressed adrenals have insufficient cortisol after exogenous prednisone is consumed in setting of stressor → insufficient alpha-1 expression on arterioles → drop in BP; hydrocortisone is Tx because without the glucocorticoid, NE and E can’t do their job.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + long-standing rheumatoid arthritis managed with multiple medications + 6-month Hx of dry cough + CXR shows reticular pattern; what’s the risk factor for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: methotrexate-induced pulmonary fibrosis + rheumatoid lung (the autoimmune disease itself, independent of methotrexate, can cause pulmonary fibrosis, so patients will have restrictive lung disease due to both methotrexate and the RA).

rapidFireQAs.q: 39F + rheumatoid arthritis + low RBCs, WBCs and platelets + splenomegaly; Q wants risk factor for this condition
rapidFireQAs.a: rheumatoid arthritis; diagnosis is Felty syndrome (RA + neutropenia + splenomegaly); sometimes RBCs and platelets can be down as well.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + BMI 40 + smoker + HTN; Q asks #1 way to decrease risk of osteoarthritis in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: weight loss (exceedingly HY).

rapidFireQAs.q: 62F + has peripheral edema + using high doses of naproxen for past 6 weeks to manage her osteoarthritis; Q wants to know #1 way to minimize risk for this patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: avoidance of NSAIDs; patient has fluid retention due to NSAIDs (decreased renal blood flow causes kidney to reabsorb fluid to compensate).

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + pregnant + fetus shows intrauterine growth restriction; risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: often uteroplacental insufficiency, e.g., from smoking, cocaine use, HTN, SLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + ovarian mass + purple discoloration of knuckles + violaceous eyelids + proximal muscle weakness; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: dermatomyositis due to ovarian cancer. Dermatomyositis usually idiopathic, but a risk factor for it that’s assessed is ovarian cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 2M + enucleation of eye for retinoblastoma; Q asks about this being risk factor for which of the following in the future?
rapidFireQAs.a: osteosarcoma; hereditary retinoblastoma can also lead to osteosarcoma. HY RISK FACTORS
